operations.name: Timofey Pavlovich Bukhanov

expected.name: Timofey Pavlovich Bukhanov
expected.description:
Timofey Pavlovich Bukhanov was born 1902 in Born , Volyn, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a laborer. Immigrated to the United States in 1909.

Nephew of URW activist Peter Bianki. In 1909 he and his sister joined their mother, Alexandra Nikiforovna Bukhanova, in the US. He graduated from high school in Manhattan in 1918 and became secretary of the Greenpoint, Brooklyn branch of the Union of Russian Workers. He was arrested during the Palmer Raids in November 1919 and became the youngest passenger deported aboard the Buford on December 21, 1919. 

After returning to Russia he was employed by the Russian-American Tool Plant (Russko-Amerikanskiy instrumental’nyy zavod). In July 1921 he signed (possibly under duress) a statement issued by the Union of Russian Anarchist Workers Repatriated from America that advocated critical support for the Soviet regime. Arrested in 1923 during a crackdown on anarchists. Married 1930s and in 1937 graduated from the Leningrad Industrial Institute with a degree in metallurgy. Assigned to a factory in Voronezh, where his mother, wife, and children joined him. Arrested in July 1938 during the Great Purge and sentenced to five years in the Tomasinlag forced labor camp, where he died November 1942.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

operations.name: Colville McBarnette

expected.name: Colville McBarnette
expected.description: Colville McBarnette was a Grenadian government or military figure imprisoned in the Grenada Seventeen case following the 1983 U.S. invasion. Amnesty International documents nine to twelve days of incommunicado U.S. military custody before transfer to Grenadian authorities. The group was later convicted in connection with the killings of Maurice Bishop and others. Amnesty classified them as political prisoners and challenged the fairness of their trial without taking a position on guilt or innocence. Associated Press reports actual release from Richmond Hill Prison on December 18, 2008.
expected.body:
U.S. military custody

Amnesty International records arrest in late October 1983 and nine to twelve days of U.S. detention, followed by handover to Grenadian and Caribbean Peacekeeping Force authorities around November 5, 1983. Individual exact endpoints have not been established. The case date is stored with month precision. The transfer was not freedom from confinement, so it is not recorded as a release date. No single day count is inferred from the reported range.

Subsequent Grenadian imprisonment

Associated Press reports actual release from Richmond Hill Prison on December 18, 2008.

The years spent in Richmond Hill Prison after handover are distinct from the U.S. military detention. They are described here and are not counted as years in U.S. custody.

Historical portrait source: “In loving memory of Kamau McBarnette,” NOW Grenada, January 14, 2021, including a tribute by fellow prisoner John Ventour. The named historical photograph is retained unchanged.

U.S. military custody ended by transfer

Amnesty International's original 2003 report, page 6, dates transfer from U.S. military detention to Grenadian and Caribbean Peacekeeping Force custody to on or around November 5, 1983. Page 2 identifies all seventeen members individually. Both original pages were rendered and visually reviewed. The U.S. case endpoint is therefore November 1983 at month precision, not an exact November 5 day and not release to freedom. Later Grenadian custody, court proceedings and actual release must remain distinct.

operations.name: Pietro Giovanni Perruchon

expected.name: Pietro Giovanni Perruchon
expected.description:
Pietro Giovanni Perruchon was born 1885 in Arnaz (Aosta), Italy. Worked as a miner. Immigrated to the United States in 1907.

Migrated to the United States in 1907, returning to Italy in 1910 before coming back to the U.S. in 1911. His wife Maria Rosa Joly joined him in 1912, and their daughter Lotta was born in 1914. Worked as a miner in Colorado and Arizona and became an anarchist before his second migration. He distributed literature and correspondence for Galleani’s Cronaca Sovversiva, published a militant antiwar article in La Questione Sociale in 1915, and belonged to the IWW’s Metal Mine Workers Industrial Union. Participated in the IWW’s 1917 miners’ strike in Globe and Miami, Arizona. Arrested March 26, 1918 in Globe for distributing radical literature and was convicted under the Espionage Act at a Tucson trial in May 1918 after a jury deliberation lasting only ninety seconds. Sentenced to two years in Leavenworth, he was detained for deportation after release and denied permission to visit his wife and daughter before removal. Deported March 27, 1920.

Back in Italy he founded the Gruppo di emancipazione in 1920 and was sentenced to five days in prison that June for violating Article 19 of the criminal code. Subscribed to Carlo Tresca’s Il Martello and Errico Malatesta’s Pensiero e Volontà. Arrested in April 1921 on suspicion of involvement in the La Diana Theater bombing, he was released in June. Migrated to France for work in 1923, returned to Italy in 1924, and went back to France in 1925, working as a chauffeur in Paris, where his adult daughter joined him. Italian authorities described him as having “demonstrated a specific tendency toward terroristic action.” In 1937 he briefly returned to Italy to claim an inheritance, was arrested, claimed to have abandoned radicalism, and was released. He spent his remaining decades in France, corresponding with Italian anarchists in the United States until his death there in 1967.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.
